from: a first month at a freight and customs desk
to: running a brokerage office and speaking for it to lines, customs houses and foreign principals
case_setting: a named part of a customs broking and freight forwarding office
series_arc: first month at the freight desk → **running an office and speaking for it abroad**
learners: They work, or are about to work, in a Syrian customs broking house, freight forwarder, shipping agency or the import–export department of a trading company or factory — where English is the language of the bill of lading, the letter of credit, the certificate of origin and the messages that arrive from a shipping line in Istanbul, a buyer in Hamburg or a bank's documentary credits department.
neutral: It is **desk-neutral within the trade**. One cohort can contain a customs clerk, a documentation assistant and a haulage coordinator, and all three practise the same skill on their own consignments.
contexts_intro: The programme assumes learners work on different parts of a shipment, not one. Twelve trade contexts carry the case studies:
contexts: The shipping line and the bill of lading
Letters of credit and the bank
The freight forwarder and the haulier
Certificates of origin and the chamber of commerce
upward: **Upward and outward paper:** delivery orders and amendment requests, claim letters to carriers and insurers, decision papers for a principal, submissions to a chamber of commerce or a customs house, terms notes after a negotiation and briefings written for three readers at once — usually written, usually read by somebody who was not there.
contact: **Line, customs and foreign-principal contact:** shipping lines and their agents, customs houses and inspectors, documentary credits departments, forwarders abroad, overseas buyers, suppliers and insurers, often where neither side is a native speaker.
reading_rows: Notes, instructions, documents, messages, tariff pages — 134–182 words
Explanations, claims, options notes, reports — 191–244 words
Decision papers, standards, submissions, hearings — 289–359 words
writing_rows: Notes, slips, logs, a three-line handover — 52–75 words
Explanations, claims, recommendations, monthly packs — 92–124 words
Decision papers, standards, appraisals, submissions — 145–194 words
move3: Decide, supervise, and speak for the office
resp2: a consignment, a document and a deadline
resp2b: a consignment, a document and a deadline
arc2: someone who owns a consignment, a document and a deadline
threads: **being honest about what you did not do and cannot evidence** (Course 1 S9 → Course 2 S14 → Course 3 S28); **giving a figure its definition, basis and weakness** (C1 S4 → C2 S16 and S20 → C3 S27); and **writing so that the reader can act** (C1 S12 → C2 S19 → C3 S25).
h1: from your first day at the freight desk to a clerk the office can rely on
h2: from dependable pair of hands to owning a consignment, a document and a deadline
h3: from owning a consignment to running an office and speaking for it to lines, customs and foreign principals
map_example: A learner on the customs desk meets their own work in sessions 2, 14 and 26, each time at a higher level of responsibility.
posts1: Customs clerk · documentation assistant · delivery order clerk · shipping clerk · yard and warehouse clerk · haulage coordinator · agency trainee taking calls and messages
gives1: Being understood in the office and at a counter, taking an instruction accurately, keeping a file and a register a second person can trust, answering for the office on the telephone, holding a rule under pressure, accounting for a consignment and handing it on
posts2: Senior customs clerk · documentation supervisor · operations clerk · claims assistant · letter of credit clerk · port office assistant · agency account handler
gives2: Owning a consignment and a document: explaining an error so a reader who was not there can follow it, training somebody on a live file, explaining why a charge moved, pressing a claim on a carrier, recommending with a reservation, and reporting upward including what did not happen
posts3: Operations manager · documentation manager · branch or port office manager · claims manager · customs manager · agency manager · deputy principal
gives3: Other people's work and the office's word: delegating, appraising, chairing the operations review, writing the standard an office follows, naming risk before it lands, negotiating with lines and insurers, disagreeing upward, and answering a chamber of commerce
constraint: a capable young broker at the clerk's grade
sub1: From your first day at the freight desk to a clerk the office can rely on
sub2: From dependable pair of hands to owning a consignment, a document and a deadline
sub3: From owning a consignment to running an office and speaking for it to lines, customs and foreign principals
arc1_text: The learner arrives in a brokerage office unable to operate, and leaves able to be relied on: to take an instruction accurately, keep a file and a register a second person can trust, answer for the office on the telephone, be trusted with documents and a counter, hold a rule under pressure when a client is shouting, account for a consignment and hand it on.
arc2_text: The learner is given something of their own — a consignment, a credit, a customs file, a claim — and learns the language that ownership requires: explaining an error so that a reader who was not there can follow it, training somebody on a live file, explaining why a charge moved, pressing a claim on a carrier, recommending with a reservation, and reporting upward including what did not happen.
arc3_text: The learner becomes answerable for other people's work and for the office's word. Three sessions are given to supervision itself — delegating, appraising and chairing — and the course runs on through writing the standard an office follows, naming risk before it lands, negotiating with lines, forwarders and insurers, answering a chamber of commerce, and arguing for the learner's own next post.
